course.title: Spanish, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Latin American Spanish from real-world basics through fluent, everyday command — real sentences, real grammar, real conversation
course.heroNative: De lo esencial a la fluidez
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, with genuine native-quality audio for every single line.

a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: me, te, se...
a2-reflexive.explanation: Many everyday Spanish verbs describing routines are reflexive: the action is done TO oneself, so a small pronoun (me/te/se/nos/se) goes right before the verb. "Levantarse" (to get (oneself) up) becomes "me levanto" (I get up), "te levantas" (you get up), "se levanta" (he/she gets up). The pronoun changes with the subject but the verb conjugates completely normally otherwise.
a2-reflexive.fact: Spanish uses reflexive verbs for far more than literal self-actions — "llamarse" (to call oneself) is simply how you say your name ("Me llamo Ana" = "My name is Ana"), and many emotional/change-of-state verbs are reflexive too ("enojarse" = to get angry, "aburrirse" = to get bored) even though English doesn't treat them as reflexive at all.

dialogue.native: ¿A qué hora te levantas?
dialogue.en: What time do you get up?

dialogue.native: Me levanto a las seis y media.
dialogue.en: I get up at six thirty.

a2-preterite.title: The Preterite: Completed Past Actions
a2-preterite.explanation: The preterite describes an action that was completed at a specific point in the past — something that started and finished, like a single event. Regular -ar verbs add -é/-aste/-ó/-amos/-aron (hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron); regular -er and -ir verbs share the same endings: -í/-iste/-ió/-imos/-ieron (comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron).
a2-preterite.fact: Many of Spanish's most common verbs are irregular in the preterite and simply have to be memorized: "ir" (to go) and "ser" (to be) share the exact same preterite forms (fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron) — context alone tells you which one is meant. "Hacer" becomes hice/hiciste/hizo/hicimos/hicieron, and "tener" becomes tuve/tuviste/tuvo/tuvimos/tuvieron.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué hiciste ayer?
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.native: Fui al cine con mis amigos.
dialogue.en: I went to the movies with my friends.

a2-imperfect.title: The Imperfect: Ongoing or Habitual Past
a2-imperfect.explanation: While the preterite marks a completed event, the imperfect describes what was ongoing, habitual, or in the background — "used to" or "was ...ing" in English. Regular -ar verbs add -aba/-abas/-aba/-ábamos/-aban (hablaba, hablabas...); -er and -ir verbs share -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-ían (comía, vivía...). Only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban), and ver (veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían).
a2-imperfect.fact: The imperfect is what sets the scene: "Cuando era niño, vivía en el campo" (When I was a child, I lived in the countryside) describes an ongoing state, not a single completed event — that's exactly why "era" and "vivía" are imperfect, not preterite. A sentence often mixes both: the imperfect describes what was happening, and the preterite marks the single event that interrupted it.

dialogue.native: ¿Cómo era tu vida cuando eras joven?
dialogue.en: What was your life like when you were young?

dialogue.native: Vivía en un pueblo pequeño y jugaba mucho afuera.
dialogue.en: I lived in a small town and played outside a lot.

a2-ser-estar.title: Ser vs. Estar: Two Ways to Say "To Be"
a2-ser-estar.pattern: ser = identity, characteristics, origin, time · estar = location, condition, ongoing states
a2-ser-estar.explanation: Spanish splits "to be" into two verbs. "Ser" is for things that define what something fundamentally IS: identity ("Soy Ana"), permanent characteristics ("Es alta"), origin ("Es de México"), profession, and time ("Son las tres"). "Estar" is for location ("Estoy en casa") and temporary states or conditions ("Estoy cansado", "La sopa está caliente").
a2-ser-estar.fact: The same adjective can take either verb with a real difference in meaning: "Ella es aburrida" means "She is boring" (a trait), while "Ella está aburrida" means "She is bored" (a temporary feeling) — one small verb swap changes the whole sentence.

dialogue.native: ¿Cómo estás?
dialogue.en: How are you (feeling)?

dialogue.native: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú de dónde eres?
dialogue.en: I'm well, thanks. And where are you from?

a2-direct-object.title: Direct Object Pronouns: lo, la, los, las
a2-direct-object.explanation: A direct object pronoun replaces the thing or person directly receiving the action, and in Spanish it goes BEFORE the conjugated verb (the opposite order from English). "Compro el pan" (I buy the bread) becomes "Lo compro" (I buy it) — "pan" is masculine so it's replaced by "lo". Feminine nouns use "la", and the plurals are "los" and "las".
a2-direct-object.fact: With two verbs together (like wanting + an infinitive), the pronoun can go in either of two places with no change in meaning: before the first verb ("Lo quiero comprar") or attached to the end of the infinitive ("Quiero comprarlo") — both mean exactly "I want to buy it".

dialogue.native: ¿Ya compraste los boletos?
dialogue.en: Did you already buy the tickets?

dialogue.native: Sí, los compré esta mañana.
dialogue.en: Yes, I bought them this morning.

a2-gustar.title: Gustar: "To Be Pleasing To"
a2-gustar.explanation: "Gustar" doesn't work like English "to like" — literally it means "to be pleasing to", so the THING liked is the grammatical subject, and the PERSON who likes it takes an indirect object pronoun. "Me gusta el café" is literally "Coffee is pleasing to me." The verb agrees with the thing liked: "gusta" for one thing, "gustan" for several ("Me gustan los libros").
a2-gustar.fact: Several other very common verbs work exactly the same way: "encantar" (to love/be delighted by), "interesar" (to interest), "molestar" (to bother), "faltar" (to be lacking) — once you understand "me gusta", all of these follow the identical [pronoun] + verb + [thing] pattern.

dialogue.native: ¿Te gusta el fútbol?
dialogue.en: Do you like soccer?

dialogue.native: Sí, me encanta. Me gustan mucho los partidos los fines de semana.
dialogue.en: Yes, I love it. I really like the games on weekends.

a2-indirect-object.title: Indirect Object Pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les
a2-indirect-object.explanation: An indirect object pronoun marks WHO receives or benefits from an action — usually the person a thing is given, told, or shown to. "Le doy el regalo a mi madre" (I give the gift to my mother) can simply be "Le doy el regalo" once context is clear — "le" already means "to her/him/you-formal". Unlike direct object pronouns, "le" and "les" don't change for gender.
a2-indirect-object.fact: "Le" is ambiguous on its own (it can mean to him, to her, or to you-formal), so Spanish often adds "a él", "a ella", or the person's name for clarity even though the pronoun is technically already there: "Le escribí una carta a mi abuela" keeps both "le" and "a mi abuela" together, which sounds redundant to English speakers but is completely normal and expected in Spanish.

dialogue.native: ¿Le compraste algo a tu hermana?
dialogue.en: Did you buy something for your sister?

dialogue.native: Sí, le compré un libro que le va a encantar.
dialogue.en: Yes, I bought her a book that she's going to love.

a2-ir-a.title: Ir a + Infinitive: Talking About the Near Future
a2-ir-a.explanation: The easiest and most common way to talk about future plans in everyday Spanish isn't a special future tense at all — it's just "ir" (to go), conjugated, plus "a", plus an infinitive: "Voy a estudiar" (I am going to study), "Vamos a viajar" (We are going to travel). It works exactly like English "going to".
a2-ir-a.fact: This construction is used constantly in spoken Latin American Spanish — far more often than the formal future tense (like "estudiaré"), which tends to sound a bit more formal or literary in everyday conversation. If you only ever learn one way to talk about the future, "ir a + infinitive" is the one that gets used the most.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.native: Voy a visitar a mis padres y vamos a cocinar juntos.
dialogue.en: I am going to visit my parents and we are going to cook together.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.explanation: To compare two things, Spanish uses "más...que" (more...than) or "menos...que" (less...than): "Mi hermano es más alto que yo" (My brother is taller than me). For equal comparisons, use "tan...como" (as...as): "Es tan inteligente como su hermana." For the superlative — the most/least of a group — add the definite article: "el más alto", "la más inteligente".
a2-comparatives.fact: A handful of common adjectives have their own irregular comparative words instead of using "más": "bueno" (good) becomes "mejor" (better), "malo" (bad) becomes "peor" (worse), and "viejo"/"joven" have both a regular form (más viejo/más joven) and, for age among people, the special words "mayor"/"menor".

dialogue.native: ¿Cuál restaurante es mejor, este o aquel?
dialogue.en: Which restaurant is better, this one or that one?

dialogue.native: Este es mejor, pero aquel es más barato.
dialogue.en: This one is better, but that one is cheaper.

b1-commands.title: Commands: Telling People What to Do
b1-commands.pattern: tú: [present-tense él/ella form] · usted: [present subjunctive] · negative: no + subjunctive
b1-commands.explanation: Informal (tú) commands mostly borrow the él/ella present-tense form: "¡Habla!" (Talk!), "¡Come!" (Eat!), "¡Escribe!" (Write!). Formal (usted) commands use the present subjunctive form instead: "¡Hable!", "¡Coma!", "¡Escriba!". Negative commands ALWAYS use the subjunctive, even for tú: "¡No hables!", "¡No comas!".
b1-commands.fact: A handful of very common verbs have irregular tú affirmative commands that don't follow the él/ella-form rule at all: "decir" → "di", "hacer" → "haz", "ir" → "ve", "poner" → "pon", "salir" → "sal", "ser" → "sé", "tener" → "ten", "venir" → "ven" — these eight are simply memorized.

dialogue.native: ¡Ven aquí y ayúdame con esto!
dialogue.en: Come here and help me with this!

dialogue.native: Ya voy, no te preocupes.
dialogue.en: I'm coming, don't worry.

b1-present-perfect.title: Present Perfect: Talking About Recent Experience
b1-present-perfect.explanation: The present perfect connects a past action to now — something that happened recently, or an experience that still matters. Form it with a conjugated form of "haber" plus the past participle: "he hablado" (I have spoken), "has comido" (you have eaten), "ha vivido" (he/she has lived). The participle never changes for gender or number here — it always ends in -ado or -ido.
b1-present-perfect.fact: Several very common verbs have irregular past participles that must be memorized: "hacer" → "hecho", "decir" → "dicho", "ver" → "visto", "poner" → "puesto", "escribir" → "escrito", "volver" → "vuelto", "abrir" → "abierto", "romper" → "roto", "morir" → "muerto".

dialogue.native: ¿Has visto la nueva película de la que todos hablan?
dialogue.en: Have you seen the new movie everyone's talking about?

dialogue.native: No, todavía no he tenido tiempo de verla.
dialogue.en: No, I haven't had time to see it yet.

b1-subjunctive-intro.title: Present Subjunctive: Wishes, Wants, and Doubts
b1-subjunctive-intro.pattern: querer/esperar/necesitar que + [subject] + subjunctive verb (-e for -ar verbs, -a for -er/-ir verbs)
b1-subjunctive-intro.explanation: When one subject wants, hopes, or needs another subject to do something, Spanish switches the second verb into the subjunctive mood after "que": "Quiero que vengas" (I want you to come), "Espero que estés bien" (I hope you're well), "Necesito que me ayudes" (I need you to help me). The subjunctive endings flip the usual pattern: -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
b1-subjunctive-intro.fact: The subjunctive is only used when the subject of "querer"/"esperar" and the subject of the second verb are DIFFERENT people. If they're the same person, Spanish just uses an infinitive instead: "Quiero ir" (I want to go — not "quiero que vaya"), but "Quiero que vayas" (I want you to go).

dialogue.native: Espero que puedas venir a mi fiesta el sábado.
dialogue.en: I hope you can come to my party on Saturday.

dialogue.native: Claro, quiero que sea una noche inolvidable.
dialogue.en: Of course, I want it to be an unforgettable night.

b1-relative-clauses.title: Relative Clauses: Connecting Ideas with que, quien, donde
b1-relative-clauses.pattern: que (that/which/who) · quien(es) (who, after a preposition) · donde (where)
b1-relative-clauses.explanation: "Que" is the all-purpose relative pronoun for both people and things: "el libro que leí" (the book that I read), "la mujer que conocí" (the woman I met). "Quien"/"quienes" refers only to people and is used mainly after a preposition: "la persona con quien hablé" (the person with whom I spoke). "Donde" replaces a place: "la casa donde nací" (the house where I was born).
b1-relative-clauses.fact: Unlike English, Spanish never drops the relative pronoun. English allows "the book I read" with no "that," but Spanish always requires "el libro que leí" — "que" can never be omitted.

dialogue.native: Esta es la ciudad donde crecí.
dialogue.en: This is the city where I grew up.

dialogue.native: ¿Y quién es esa persona con quien estás hablando?
dialogue.en: And who is that person you're talking with?

b1-por-para.title: Por vs Para: Two Words for 'For'
b1-por-para.explanation: "Por" looks backward to a cause, means, or exchange: "Gracias por tu ayuda" (thanks for your help — cause), "Viajamos por tren" (we traveled by train — means), "Pagué veinte dólares por el libro" (I paid twenty dollars for the book — exchange). "Para" looks forward to a purpose, destination, or deadline: "Este regalo es para ti" (this gift is for you — recipient), "Salgo para Madrid mañana" (I leave for Madrid tomorrow — destination), "Necesito esto para el lunes" (I need this by Monday — deadline).
b1-por-para.fact: A useful shortcut: "por" often answers "why/how," while "para" answers "for what purpose/for whom." "Trabajo por dinero" (I work because of/for the sake of money) versus "Trabajo para una empresa grande" (I work for a big company — the employer, not the motive).

dialogue.native: ¿Para quién es este paquete?
dialogue.en: Who is this package for?

dialogue.native: Es para mi madre, lo compré por su cumpleaños.
dialogue.en: It's for my mother, I bought it for her birthday.

b1-past-perfect.title: Past Perfect: An Action Before Another Past Action
b1-past-perfect.explanation: The past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) describes something that had already happened before another point in the past: "Cuando llegué, ya habían empezado la reunión" (when I arrived, they had already started the meeting). It's built with the imperfect of "haber" plus the past participle, and it's what lets you clearly sequence two past events.
b1-past-perfect.fact: The same irregular participles from the present perfect carry over unchanged: "había hecho", "había visto", "había dicho", "había puesto" — if you know the present perfect's irregulars, the past perfect uses exactly the same set.

dialogue.native: Cuando llegamos al cine, la película ya había comenzado.
dialogue.en: When we got to the movies, the film had already started.

dialogue.native: ¡Qué mal! Nunca había llegado tan tarde.
dialogue.en: That's too bad! I had never arrived so late.

lessons.title: The Letter I Never Sent
lessons.description: A reflective, slightly emotional story about regret and relative clauses.

readingPassage.context: A reflective, slightly emotional story about regret and relative clauses.

paragraphs.native: Hace años escribí una carta para una persona a quien nunca le dije la verdad.
paragraphs.en: Years ago I wrote a letter for a person to whom I never told the truth.

paragraphs.native: En ella explicaba todo lo que había sentido pero nunca había expresado en voz alta.
paragraphs.en: In it I explained everything I had felt but had never expressed out loud.

paragraphs.native: Al final, decidí no enviarla porque tenía miedo de su reacción.
paragraphs.en: In the end, I decided not to send it because I was afraid of her reaction.

paragraphs.native: Ahora que ha pasado tanto tiempo, a veces me pregunto qué habría pasado.
paragraphs.en: Now that so much time has passed, sometimes I wonder what would have happened.

paragraphs.native: Es probable que nunca sepa la respuesta, pero al menos aprendí a ser más honesto.
paragraphs.en: It's likely I'll never know the answer, but at least I learned to be more honest.

lessons.description: A capstone reflective story reviewing B1's key grammar in context.

readingPassage.context: A capstone reflective story reviewing B1's key grammar in context.

paragraphs.native: Este año ha sido lleno de cambios que nunca había imaginado.
paragraphs.en: This year has been full of changes I had never imagined.

paragraphs.native: He aprendido a confiar más en las personas que realmente me apoyan.
paragraphs.en: I've learned to trust more in the people who truly support me.

paragraphs.native: Espero que el próximo año traiga tantas sorpresas buenas como este.
paragraphs.en: I hope next year brings as many good surprises as this one.

paragraphs.native: La ciudad donde vivo ahora se ha convertido en un verdadero hogar para mí.
paragraphs.en: The city where I now live has become a true home for me.

paragraphs.native: Al mirar atrás, me doy cuenta de que cada desafío me ha hecho más fuerte.
paragraphs.en: Looking back, I realize that every challenge has made me stronger.
